summary: Fox Point, at the entrance to St. Anthony Harbour in Newfoundland: a harbour light from 1906, an iron tower from 1912, and a staffed Coast Guard station today.

structures.note: Built 2002/2003 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett 2002-03). Rowlett gives the tower as 8 m (26 ft).

staffing.note: Three keepers at the site (Town of St. Anthony, 2020); the DFO brochure lists it among 23 staffed lightstations.

access.note: Working Canadian Coast Guard lightstation. Grounds open, tower closed.

events.note: Harbour light: lens lantern on an open white framework, lit through the navigation season
Harbour light replaced by an iron occulting light tower
Iron light tower, light 20.5 m above the sea
Bungalow, landing and storehouse; a second dwelling in the early 1960s
Iron tower replaced by a combined light tower and fog alarm building; focal plane 26.8 m
Old iron tower lowered over the cliff, jammed and was later washed away
Acetylene light converted to station-generated electricity
Commercial power brought to the station; keepers no longer tended the light at night
De-staffed in July 1992 because of automation (Town of St. Anthony, marker)
Modern lighthouse dating from 2002/2003, with a small office nearby

corrections.why: The lighthouse is owned by the Canadian Coast Guard (LighthouseFriends). The café (the Lightkeepers restaurant) is a business in a former keeper's house; Rowlett lists it as 'site manager', which is the source of the record's value.
A harbour light was established on the point in 1906, and the iron tower followed in 1912 (LighthouseFriends, the Town, the marker).
In 1960 the iron tower was replaced by a combined light and fog alarm building; the light stayed in service.
The light is active on the Coast Guard list and the 2002/2003 tower is the modern light. Nothing in the sources supports a deactivation in 2003.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata's 2003 and Rowlett's 1912 are both partly right: the first light on the point was a harbour light in 1906 (LighthouseFriends, the Town, the marker), the first iron tower was 1912, and the modern tower is 2002/2003.

The 20.5 m (67 ft) figure belongs to the 1912 tower (LighthouseFriends, Town, marker). The 26.8 m figure belongs to the 1960 light and is the current Coast Guard figure (LighthouseFriends, Coast Guard list).

notes_for_editor: Thin on primary records. No Canadian or Newfoundland government report on the 1906 harbour light or the 1912 tower was found: the Canadian Marine reports in the local corpus (1900-1924) hold no entry for this St. Anthony light, and Newfoundland's own lighthouse records before 1949 were not reached. The story rests on LighthouseFriends (registry facts, copyrighted: only one sentence quoted, in the Pynn passage), the Town of St. Anthony's page (information from the Coast Guard), the 1960s-era marker text on HMDB, the Coast Guard list (current characteristic, focal height, range) and the DFO brochure. Disagreements left open: (1) the 1912 light's characteristic (2.5 s occulting per LighthouseFriends) against the current Fl W 10s (Coast Guard) and Rowlett's 'white flash every 15 s'; (2) the fog alarm date, 1952 (marker) or 1958 (Town); (3) the 1960 structure's shape (LighthouseFriends square tower, Rowlett skeletal tower under white siding); (4) tower height, 9.3 m (Coast Guard list), 8 m (Rowlett), 8.0 m (Wikidata). Staffing: the DFO brochure is dated 2005 and lists Fox Point as staffed; LighthouseFriends says keepers no longer live on the point; the Town says three keepers in 2020. Confirm current staffing with the Coast Guard before the page says more. The keepers 'W. Patey', 'Joseph Boyd', 'Wesley Pynn' and 'B.S. Pynn' come from LighthouseFriends and the marker, not from a government list. The marker's 'W. and B.S. Pynn' may or may not be the same Wesley Pynn; the story does not link them. Recent keepers named in LighthouseFriends (2009) are left unnamed. The Lightkeepers restaurant is a business and is named only as the former dwelling's use. The Wikipedia article on Fox Point (the settlement) was not used. Checker pass 2026-10-28: the 1912 light's visibility is kept in the source's own unit (10 miles), not converted to nautical miles. The DFO brochure is dated 2005 and is cited as such. Staffing after 2020 is unconfirmed.
